mcqs.question: A secret is committed to a git repository and removed in the very next commit. Is it still exposed?
options: Yes — the secret remains in the repository's history and is retrievable by anyone with read access to that history
No — deleting the file in a follow-up commit fully removes it from the repository
Only if the repository is public, never in a private repository
No, as long as the removal commit happens within the same day
mcqs.explanation: Git history is permanent by default — removing a file in a later commit doesn't erase it from earlier commits, so anyone who can read the repo's history can still retrieve it. This is true for private repos too, and there's no time window after which a committed secret becomes safe on its own.

mcqs.question: What does a secrets manager provide that a shared config file storing the same secret cannot?
options: Faster read performance for the application at runtime
Automatic encryption of all application code, not just secrets
Per-secret, per-identity access control and an audit log of who accessed which secret and when
The ability to store secrets without any authentication at all
mcqs.explanation: A config file grants access to whoever can read the file; a vault can scope access to a specific identity and specific secret, and log every access — that access control and auditability is the core advantage. It's not primarily a performance feature, doesn't encrypt application code, and access control (not the absence of it) is the whole point.

mcqs.question: A vault generates a unique, time-limited database credential each time a service requests one, rather than handing out one shared password. What's the main security benefit of this dynamic-secret approach?
options: It makes the database itself run faster
It removes the need for the database to authenticate connections at all
It eliminates the need for network encryption between the service and the database
A leak from one consumer doesn't expose every other consumer's access, since each credential is unique and expires on its own
mcqs.explanation: Unique, short-lived credentials per consumer mean a single leaked credential has a narrow, time-boxed impact rather than compromising every service sharing one static password. Dynamic secrets don't affect database performance, don't remove the need for authentication, and don't substitute for transport encryption.

mcqs.question: Why does scheduled rotation matter even when a team has no evidence any secret has been compromised?
options: It limits how long an undetected leak — one the team doesn't know has happened — can remain valid, since it doesn't depend on detecting anything
It replaces the need for access control on the secrets manager
It is required by every cloud provider's terms of service
It eliminates the need for compromise-triggered rotation entirely
mcqs.explanation: Scheduled rotation's value is precisely that it doesn't require detecting a leak — it bounds the exposure window for leaks nobody has noticed yet. It doesn't replace access control, isn't a universal provider requirement, and compromise-triggered rotation is still needed for leaks that are actually detected, since waiting for the next scheduled cycle would leave a known exposure open.

mcqs.question: A team assumes their staging database credential is low-risk because "it's just staging." Why can this assumption be dangerous?
options: Staging credentials are technically identical to production credentials in every cloud provider
If staging shares any network path or data with production, a leaked staging credential can become a production-impacting incident despite being treated as lower-stakes
Staging environments never contain any secrets, so there is nothing to leak
Vaults cannot be configured to separate staging and production secrets
mcqs.explanation: A staging secret being treated as low-stakes doesn't make its blast radius small if staging has any real connectivity or data overlap with production — a common shortcut that undermines the assumption. Staging and production credentials are distinct by design, staging environments do hold real secrets, and vaults fully support environment-scoped separation.

mcqs.question: After a leaked database password is discovered, a team generates a new password and updates all known services, but never explicitly revokes the old one. What's the risk?
options: None — generating a new password automatically invalidates every previous one
The old, leaked password may still be valid, so an attacker who has it is unaffected by the rotation
The new password will fail to work until the old one is manually deleted
This only matters if the leak was publicly disclosed
mcqs.explanation: Rotation is a two-part operation — issuing a new secret doesn't automatically invalidate the old one unless it's explicitly revoked, so an attacker holding the leaked credential can keep using it until that revocation happens. New and old passwords typically coexist until revoked, and the risk exists whether or not the leak became public.
